quiz.title: Exercise 5.4 Quiz: Exponential & Logarithmic Derivatives
quiz.intro: Eight questions on differentiating exponential and logarithmic functions, the core of NCERT Exercise 5.4. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 12 Continuity and Differentiability, Exercise 5.4

questions.explanation: The exponential function e<sup>x</sup> is its own derivative: d/dx (e<sup>x</sup>) = e<sup>x</sup>.

questions.q: What is d/dx (log x) for x > 0?
questions.explanation: The derivative of the natural logarithm is 1/x, valid for x > 0.

questions.q: Differentiate a<sup>x</sup> with respect to x (a > 0).
questions.explanation: Writing a<sup>x</sup> = e<sup>x log a</sup> and using the chain rule gives d/dx (a<sup>x</sup>) = a<sup>x</sup> log a.
By the chain rule, differentiate the exponential and multiply by the derivative of sin x: e<sup>sin x</sup> · cos x.
d/dx log(sin x) = (1/sin x) · cos x = cos x / sin x = cot x.
Use the product rule: e<sup>x</sup> log x + e<sup>x</sup>(1/x) = e<sup>x</sup>(log x + 1/x).
Chain rule twice: (1/cos e<sup>x</sup>) · (-sin e<sup>x</sup>) · e<sup>x</sup> = -e<sup>x</sup> tan e<sup>x</sup>.

questions.q: What is d/dx (e<sup>x</sup> + e<sup>x<sup>2</sup></sup> + ... up to e<sup>x<sup>5</sup></sup>), evaluated for the term e<sup>x<sup>3</sup></sup> alone?
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, d/dx (e<sup>x<sup>3</sup></sup>) = e<sup>x<sup>3</sup></sup> · 3x<sup>2</sup> = 3x<sup>2</sup> e<sup>x<sup>3</sup></sup>.

faq.q: What does Exercise 5.4 of Class 12 Maths cover?
faq.a: Exercise 5.4 is about differentiating exponential and logarithmic functions — d/dx of e<sup>x</sup>, a<sup>x</sup>, log x and composite forms like e<sup>sin x</sup> or log(cos e<sup>x</sup>). Most problems combine these with the chain, product and quotient rules.

faq.q: How is Exercise 5.4 different from Exercise 5.5?
faq.a: Exercise 5.4 differentiates functions that already contain e<sup>x</sup> or log x directly. Exercise 5.5 uses logarithmic differentiation, where you take a log of both sides first — useful for powers like x<sup>x</sup> where the variable appears in both base and exponent.

faq.q: Why does the derivative of a<sup>x</sup> include log a?
faq.a: Because a<sup>x</sup> can be rewritten as e<sup>x log a</sup>. Differentiating with the chain rule brings down the constant log a, giving a<sup>x</sup> log a. Only when a = e does log a become 1, so e<sup>x</sup> is its own derivative.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in this exercise?
faq.a: Forgetting the inner derivative in the chain rule. For log(sin x) students often write 1/sin x and stop, but you must also multiply by cos x to get cot x. Always differentiate the inside function too.
